notes.meaning: The Philistines, Israel's old enemies, came back for war. They camped on land that belonged to the tribe of Judah. Older commentators think they had heard that Samuel had left Saul and that Saul was troubled and unfit to lead, so they saw their chance. The enemies of God's people look for openings, and the best opening comes when leaders have pushed away God's Spirit and his prophets.

Saul gathered Israel's army in the Valley of Elah. The name means a valley of terebinths, a kind of large shady tree. The two armies stood on two hills facing each other, with the valley between them. They were close enough to see each other and shout across.

A "champion" here means "the man between two." He was a fighter who stood between the armies and fought alone for his whole side. Goliath came from Gath, where a race of giants called the Anakim had lived since Joshua's day. Six cubits and a span is about nine feet nine inches, and some older writers reckon even taller.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), the Dead Sea Scrolls and Josephus read "four cubits and a span." That would make Goliath about six feet nine inches, still a giant in that day.

notes.meaning: Goliath was covered in bronze. His coat was made of bronze plates that overlapped like the scales of a fish. Older commentators guess it weighed somewhere between about 78 and 156 pounds. He also wore bronze guards on his shins and carried a bronze javelin slung across his back.

The wooden shaft of his spear was as thick as the beam of a weaver's loom. Its iron point alone weighed about eighteen or nineteen pounds. A helper carried his shield in front of him, probably more for show than need, since he was already covered in bronze.

Goliath shouted a challenge. Instead of a full battle, one man from each side would fight, and the loser's nation would serve the winner's. He sneered that Israel were only "servants of Saul," no better than slaves. Older commentators think this was just bragging, since no nation would really risk everything on one man. In fact, the Philistines did not keep the deal after he died.
To "defy" is to mock and shame. Goliath's taunt left Israel exposed, because no one dared to answer him. Throwing insults at the enemy before a fight was a common custom in the ancient world.

Saul and all Israel were terrified. Matthew Henry notes that when the Spirit of the Lord was on Saul he was bold, but now that the Spirit had left him, one giant's words shook him. The people lost heart because their leader did. Even brave Jonathan held back, because God had saved this honour for David. Even the bravest people are only what God makes them.

The story now turns to David. He was the son of Jesse, an Ephrathite (a man from the old clan name for the Bethlehem area) of Bethlehem in Judah. Jesse had eight sons. He was too old to go to war himself.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Adam Clarke notes that verses 12-31 are missing from the main early copies of the Greek Old Testament. Some scholars think these verses were added later, and that the story reads smoothly from verse 11 to verse 32 without them.

notes.meaning: Jesse's three oldest sons, Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah, had gone with Saul to war. David, the youngest, went back and forth between Saul's court and his father's sheep. Saul let him go home and sent for him when he was needed. Matthew Henry sees humility here: David had tasted life at court, yet he gladly went back to the hard, quiet work of a shepherd.

For forty days Goliath came out every morning and evening with his challenge. Saul waited all that time for someone to volunteer. Matthew Henry says Goliath grew prouder and Israel grew more afraid. Meanwhile God was getting ready to make the rescue all the more glorious.

Soldiers then got their food from their families at home, so Jesse sent David with grain and bread for his brothers. He also sent cheese for their commander, likely to win his kindness toward them. David was to bring back some token that his brothers were alive and well. Jesse meant only to look after his sons, but God was using this errand for a much bigger purpose.

These are still Jesse's words, telling David where to find his brothers. "Fighting" here means they were lined up and ready to fight. So far there had been no real battle, only Goliath's daily taunts.

David got up early and made sure his sheep had someone to watch them. Matthew Henry says he was faithful in small things, and so fit to be trusted with great ones. He reached the camp just as the armies lined up and shouted their battle cry. Jesse could not have planned that timing, but God arranged it.

David left the supplies with the man in charge of the baggage. Then he ran to the battle line to greet his brothers. Matthew Henry notes that he took care of what was trusted to him, and still had energy to run after a long, loaded journey.

While David talked with his brothers, Goliath came out and shouted the same challenge as before (vv. 8-9). This time David heard it. Matthew Henry says Goliath thought he was chasing glory, but he was really walking toward his own downfall.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some point out a puzzle: in the Hebrew, 2 Samuel 21:19 says Elhanan killed "Goliath of Gath." The BSB translates that verse as "the brother of Goliath."

notes.meaning: The moment the Israelite soldiers saw Goliath, they ran in terror. Matthew Henry and Wesley say one Philistine could never have scared off thousands of Israelites unless God, their Rock, had left them because they had left him (Deuteronomy 32:30).

The soldiers talked about Saul's reward for whoever killed Goliath. The winner would get great riches and the king's daughter in marriage, and his family would be freed from taxes and public duties. Saul was the tallest man in Israel, yet with God's Spirit gone from him, he dared not fight himself. Keil and Delitzsch think Saul really made these promises but later did not feel bound to keep them.

Matthew Henry says David asked about the reward not out of greed. He wanted his concern for God's honour to reach Saul. Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant, his special promise-bond with Israel, so calling Goliath "uncircumcised" meant he stood outside that covenant. David alone saw the real issue: Goliath was insulting the living God, not some idol.
The men repeated the offer to David. This shows the promise was well known in the camp. Matthew Henry notes that David went on asking others too (v. 30), hoping word of his zeal would reach the king.

Eliab, the oldest brother, flared up in anger. Matthew Henry sees jealousy: David was saying bold things Eliab himself did not dare to say. Eliab sneered about "those few sheep" and called David proud and wicked, even though David had left the flock in good hands and came because his father sent him. Keil and Delitzsch note that the pride Eliab charged David with showed most clearly in Eliab himself.

David answered gently: he had only asked a question. Older translations read "Is there not a cause?" Matthew Henry takes that to mean his father had sent him, and Israel's honour had been insulted; the Geneva Notes add that God's Spirit was stirring him. David did not trade insults, and Matthew Henry says this victory over his own temper was in some ways greater than his victory over Goliath. People who take on God's work should expect scorn even from family, and keep going humbly.
